intro.text: Six pages for the people who worked beside Paul: Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, Apollos, and Priscilla with Aquila. None of them is called one of the Twelve, and none has a calling scene in the Gospels.
Acts tells most of what is known of Silas, Timothy, Apollos, Priscilla and Aquila. Titus is never named in Acts, and Luke never in any narrative: Scripture knows both only from Paul's letters.

Paul names them with warmth: Timothy “my own son in the faith”, Titus “my partner and fellowhelper”, Luke “the beloved physician”, Priscilla and Aquila “my helpers in Christ Jesus”, Apollos “our brother”.

Later church writers made several of them bishops (Timothy of Ephesus and Titus of Crete in Eusebius, about 325; Silas of Corinth and Apollos of Caesarea in a list ascribed to Hippolytus, of unknown date) and gave some of them deaths. Every such line on these pages says who first said it and when.
McGiffert (1890) warns that such titles carry a later office back into the first century.

apostles.name: Silas
apostles.title: A chief man among the brethren, and a prophet (Acts 15:22, 32)
apostles.tagline: Sent from Jerusalem with the council's letter; Paul's partner in Macedonia.

home.text: One of the “chief men among the brethren” in the church at Jerusalem, chosen by the apostles, elders and whole church to go to Antioch.

identifications.text: Acts always calls him Silas; Paul's letters and 1 Peter call him Silvanus. Both names stand in the same company: Paul, Silas and Timothy in Macedonia and Corinth (Acts 17:14; 18:5), and “me and Silvanus and Timotheus” at Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19).

Silas and Silvanus are generally taken as one man, Silas being a short form of Silvanus (Smith 1884; Easton 1897; Kerr in the ISBE, 1915). Ramsay (1895) notes that Luke uses the everyday short forms, Silas and Priscilla, where Paul writes Silvanus and Prisca. This page relies on that identification.

Whether the Silvanus “by” whom 1 Peter was written (1 Peter 5:12) is the same man Smith (1884) calls “doubtful”, though “the probabilities are in favor of the identity”; Moorehead (ISBE, 1915) takes him to be Paul's companion.

Paul writes that “we” might have been burdensome “as the apostles of Christ” in a letter sent by Paul, Silvanus and Timotheus. Lightfoot (1890) thinks Silvanus is probably included among these “apostles”, but not Timothy, whom Paul elsewhere calls “the brother”.
That Silas was a Roman citizen rests on Paul's words at Philippi, “being Romans”, said of himself and Silas (Smith 1884; Kerr, ISBE 1915).

quote.text: Then pleased it the apostles and elders, with the whole church, to send chosen men of their own company to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas; namely, Judas surnamed Barsabas, and Silas, chief men among the brethren:

claim.text: With Judas Barsabas he carried the council's letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia, to “tell you the same things by mouth”; at Antioch the two, “being prophets also themselves”, exhorted and strengthened the brethren.

quote.text: And Paul chose Silas, and departed, being recommended by the brethren unto the grace of God.

claim.text: After Paul and Barnabas parted over John Mark, Paul chose Silas and went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.

acts.text: He was chosen with Judas Barsabas, carried the council's letter to Antioch, and with Judas exhorted the brethren there “with many words”.

The KJV goes on: “Notwithstanding it pleased Silas to abide there still” (Acts 15:34). That verse is in the Textus Receptus behind the KJV; the site's Tischendorf Greek text and the Revised Version (1881) leave it out.
Chosen by Paul, he went through Syria and Cilicia, and on through Derbe and Lystra, where Timothy joined them, delivering the decrees of the apostles and elders.

At Philippi he and Paul were seized, beaten with many stripes and put in the stocks; at midnight they “prayed, and sang praises unto God”; after the earthquake the jailor fell down before them and was baptized with his house.
Next morning Paul refused to be let out secretly: “They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans”. The magistrates came, “and they feared, when they heard that they were Romans”.
At Thessalonica some believed and “consorted with Paul and Silas”; after the uproar at Jason's house the brethren sent the two away by night to Berea.
At Berea Silas and Timothy stayed when Paul was sent on to Athens; Paul sent word for them to come “with all speed”, and they reached him at Corinth, coming “from Macedonia”.
Paul reminds the Corinthians that Christ “was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus”.
Both letters to the Thessalonians open “Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus”.
1 Peter closes: “By Silvanus, a faithful brother unto you, as I suppose, I have written briefly”.
Acts names Silas for the last time at Corinth (Acts 18:5); after that he is named only in the letters.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: A leading man of the church here.

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.note: Brought the council's letter; set out from here with Paul.

places.name: Lystra
places.note: Paul found Timothy here or at Derbe (Acts 16:1).

places.name: Philippi
places.note: Beaten and imprisoned with Paul.

places.name: Thessalonica
places.note: Also, in a list ascribed to Hippolytus, the see of a “Silvanus” counted as a different man (tradition).

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Preached here with Paul and Timothy. Called its bishop in the list ascribed to Hippolytus (tradition).

claim.text: Chose him for the second journey; they were beaten, jailed and freed together at Philippi.
Sent with him from Jerusalem; both were prophets.
Went with them to Antioch with the council's letter.
Joined them at Derbe and Lystra; stayed with Silas at Berea; named with him in the letters to the Thessalonians.
Paul and Silas went to her house when they left the prison.
Received them at Thessalonica and was dragged before the rulers for it.
1 Peter was written “by Silvanus”; that this is Paul's Silas is an identification (Smith 1884; Moorehead, ISBE 1915).

scripture.text: The last we read of him: Acts leaves him at Corinth (Acts 18:5); 1 Peter names a Silvanus as “a faithful brother” (1 Peter 5:12). Scripture does not record where he went or how he died.

tradition.text: A list of “the Seventy” ascribed to Hippolytus names “Silas, bishop of Corinth” and, as a separate man, “Silvanus, bishop of Thessalonica”. Its ANF editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”.
tradition.who: On the Seventy Apostles, ascribed to Hippolytus
tradition.when: date unknown; the text's own editor judges it spurious but old

tradition.text: Smith (1884) calls the bishopric of Corinth “A tradition of very slight authority”.

questions.question: Are Silas (Acts) and Silvanus (the letters) one man? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: One man: Silas is short for Silvanus
views.holders: Smith (1884); Easton (1897); Ramsay (1895); Kerr, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: The two names appear with the same companions in the same places: Silas with Paul and Timothy at Corinth in Acts, Silvanus with Paul and Timothy at Corinth in 2 Corinthians and the letters to the Thessalonians. Ramsay explains the difference as Luke's habit of using the everyday short form.

views.label: Two men
views.holders: the list “On the Seventy Apostles” ascribed to Hippolytus (date unknown)

argument.text: It lists “Silas, bishop of Corinth” and “Silvanus, bishop of Thessalonica” as two of the Seventy. It gives no reasons.

questions.question: Did Silas stay at Antioch after the council's letter was delivered, or go back to Jerusalem? (In the order the readings are found.)

views.label: He stayed at Antioch
views.holders: the reading of Acts 15:34 kept in the KJV; “held by some” (Kerr, ISBE 1915)

argument.text: Acts 15:34 says “it pleased Silas to abide there still”, so Paul could choose him at Antioch (Acts 15:40).

views.label: He went back to Jerusalem and later returned
views.holders: Smith (1884); Wendt and others, as reported by Kerr (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Acts 15:33 says the messengers “were let go in peace … unto the apostles”, and the principal texts (followed by the Revised Version) lack verse 34. Smith concludes Silas “must, however, have immediately revisited Antioch”.

questions.question: What did Silvanus do for 1 Peter (“By Silvanus … I have written briefly”, 1 Peter 5:12)?

views.label: He carried the letter
views.holders: Moorehead, ISBE (1915); Kühl, as reported by Bigg (1901)

argument.text: Moorehead: “The statement denotes rather the bearer than the writer or secretary.”

views.label: He helped write it, and probably carried it too
views.holders: Bigg (1901)

argument.text: Bigg thinks the letter's Greek is the work of an “interpreter”, “more probable” Silvanus than Mark, and that he “might be, and probably was, the bearer as well as the draughtsman of the Epistle”.

notSaid: Scripture names no family of Silas and does not say where he was born.

Scripture does not say whether Silas stayed at Antioch or went back to Jerusalem: the verse that says he stayed (Acts 15:34) is in the KJV but not in the site's Tischendorf Greek text or the Revised Version.
Scripture does not say where Silas went after Corinth, or how or when he died.
Scripture does not say plainly that the Silvanus of 1 Peter is Paul's companion.

apostles.name: Timothy
apostles.title: Paul's “own son in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2)
apostles.tagline: A young disciple who served Paul “as a son with the father”.

home.text: Paul found him at Derbe and Lystra: “a certain disciple was there, named Timotheus”, “well reported of by the brethren that were at Lystra and Iconium”.

family.text: His mother was “a Jewess, and believed”; his father “was a Greek”.
Paul remembers “the unfeigned faith” that dwelt first in “thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice”.
“From a child thou hast known the holy scriptures.”
Paul calls him “my beloved son, and faithful in the Lord”, “my own son in the faith” and “my dearly beloved son”.

identifications.text: The KJV spells his name Timotheus in Acts and most letters and Timothy in others (for example 2 Corinthians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 1:2); it is one Greek name.

Easton (1897), Smith (1884) and Rutherfurd (ISBE, 1915) take Paul's “own son in the faith” to mean Paul brought him to faith, probably at Lystra on the first journey, when Timothy saw the persecutions Paul names “at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra”.
Hebrews names “our brother Timothy” as “set at liberty” without saying more; Rutherfurd (ISBE, 1915) takes this to be Paul's Timothy, and adds that Hebrews was not written by Paul.
Lightfoot (1890) holds that Timothy is not called an apostle: Paul writes “Paul, an apostle … and Timothy our brother”.

quote.text: Him would Paul have to go forth with him; and took and circumcised him because of the Jews which were in those quarters: for they knew all that his father was a Greek.

claim.text: Found at Derbe and Lystra and well spoken of by the brethren, he set out with Paul and Silas as they delivered the decrees of the apostles and elders to the churches.

calling.label: 1 and 2 Timothy: hands laid on him

quote.text: Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.

claim.text: Paul recalls “the prophecies which went before on thee” and “the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands”.

acts.text: Paul circumcised him “because of the Jews which were in those quarters”, and he travelled with Paul and Silas through the cities.
At Berea he and Silas stayed behind when Paul was sent to Athens; they were told to come “with all speed”, and came “from Macedonia” to Paul at Corinth.

Paul writes that from Athens “we … sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ” to Thessalonica, and that he came back with “good tidings of your faith and charity”.
Acts does not mention Timothy at Athens; 1 Thessalonians says he was sent from there.
Smith (1884) and Rutherfurd (ISBE, 1915) take it that he came to Athens and was sent back to Thessalonica.
At Corinth he preached with Paul and Silvanus, and he is named with Paul and Silvanus in both letters to the Thessalonians.
From Ephesus Paul sent “Timotheus and Erastus” into Macedonia, and sent him on to Corinth: “Let no man therefore despise him”.
He is named with Paul at the head of 2 Corinthians, and he sends greetings in Romans: “Timotheus my workfellow”.
He was among those who went ahead of Paul to Troas on the way to Jerusalem.

He is named with Paul in the letters Paul wrote as a prisoner: Philippians, Colossians and Philemon. Paul planned to send him to Philippi: “I have no man likeminded”; “as a son with the father, he hath served with me in the gospel”.
1 Timothy says Paul asked him “to abide still at Ephesus” when Paul went into Macedonia, to charge some “that they teach no other doctrine”; Paul tells him, “Let no man despise thy youth”.
Paul tells him to “use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities”.
In 2 Timothy Paul, a prisoner, remembers his tears and asks him to come “shortly” and “before winter”, bringing Mark, the cloak left at Troas, the books and the parchments.
Hebrews says: “Know ye that our brother Timothy is set at liberty; with whom, if he come shortly, I will see you.”

places.name: Lystra
places.note: Paul found him at Derbe and Lystra (Acts 16:1); Rutherfurd (ISBE) and Easton take Lystra as his home.

places.name: Iconium
places.note: Its brethren spoke well of him.

places.name: Berea
places.note: Stayed here with Silas.

places.name: Athens
places.note: Sent from here to Thessalonica.

places.name: Thessalonica
places.note: Sent to strengthen the church.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Preached here; sent back later.

places.name: Macedonia
places.note: Sent ahead of Paul with Erastus.

places.name: Troas
places.note: Waited here for Paul.

places.name: Philippi
places.note: Paul hoped to send him here.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Asked to stay here (1 Timothy 1:3). Called its first bishop by Eusebius (about 325) and the Apostolic Constitutions (4th century or earlier) (tradition).

claim.text: Took him with him on his journey; called him “my beloved son”; named him beside himself at the head of six letters, and wrote two to him.
Travelled and waited with him at Berea; came with him to Corinth.
Sent into Macedonia with him.

person.name: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Tychicus and Trophimus

claim.text: Went with him ahead of Paul to Troas.
His mother, a believing Jewess.
His grandmother, in whom the same faith dwelt first.
Paul asks Timothy to bring him: “he is profitable to me for the ministry”.

scripture.text: In 2 Timothy Paul asks him twice to come quickly; Scripture does not say whether he reached Paul.
Hebrews reports that “our brother Timothy is set at liberty”; it does not say from what, or where he went next.

tradition.text: Eusebius writes: “Timothy, so it is recorded, was the first to receive the episcopate of the parish in Ephesus”.
The Apostolic Constitutions list among bishops ordained by the apostles: “Of Ephesus, Timotheus, ordained by Paul”.
tradition.when: a compilation its ANF editor places “not later than the fourth century”

tradition.text: That he died a martyr under Domitian is recorded by Nicephorus, “upon what authority we do not know”, as McGiffert notes; Smith (1884) reports the old traditions as “a martyr's death under Domitian or Nerva”.
tradition.who: Nicephorus Callistus, Church History 3.11 (as reported by McGiffert)

tradition.text: McGiffert (1890) calls the title “bishop of Ephesus” the “customary but unwarranted carrying back into the first century” of an office known only from the second.
tradition.who: A. C. McGiffert, note on Eusebius 3.4

questions.question: Was Timothy from Lystra or Derbe? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: Lystra
views.holders: Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915); Easton (1897)

argument.text: Acts 20:4 lists “Gaius of Derbe, and Timotheus”, as if Timothy were not of Derbe, and the brethren who spoke for him were “at Lystra and Iconium”.

views.label: Acts leaves it open
views.holders: Smith (1884)

argument.text: Smith: “The language of the Acts leaves it uncertain whether Lystra or Derbe was the residence of the devout family.”

questions.question: Was Timothy bishop of Ephesus? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes, its first bishop
views.holders: Eusebius (about 325), “so it is recorded”; the Apostolic Constitutions (not later than the 4th century)

argument.text: Eusebius names him the first bishop of Ephesus; the Apostolic Constitutions say he was “ordained by Paul”. 1 Timothy shows Paul leaving him there.

views.label: He was Paul's delegate there, not a bishop in the later sense
views.holders: McGiffert (1890); Zahn, as quoted by Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: McGiffert: the tradition “seems to be no more than a conclusion drawn from the Epistles to Timothy”, though he grants that Eusebius's “so it is recorded” suggests some authority. Zahn (as quoted by Rutherfurd, ISBE 1915): Timothy acted as “a temporary representative of Paul” at Ephesus, as he had at Corinth, Thessalonica and Philippi.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Timothy's father.
Scripture does not say when or how Timothy first believed, though Paul calls him his son in the faith.
Scripture does not say whether Timothy reached Paul in Rome before Paul's death.
Hebrews does not say where or why Timothy had been held, or who wrote the words about him.
Scripture does not record Timothy's death.

apostles.name: Titus
apostles.title: Paul's “partner and fellowhelper” (2 Corinthians 8:23)
apostles.tagline: A Greek believer, Paul's envoy to Corinth, left in Crete.

family.text: “Titus, who was with me, being a Greek”.
Paul calls him “mine own son after the common faith” and “Titus my brother”.

identifications.text: Acts never names Titus. Everything Scripture says of him is in Galatians, 2 Corinthians, 2 Timothy and the letter addressed to him.
Smith (1884) and Rutherfurd (ISBE, 1915) take “mine own son after the common faith” to mean that Paul brought him to faith.

Smith (1884) mentions that the “Titus Justus” of Acts 18:7 in the Revised Version is “possibly the same”; the KJV there reads only “Justus”. Kerr (ISBE, 1915) calls a suggested identification of Titus with Silas “very improbable”. This page relies on neither.

quote.text: Then fourteen years after I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and took Titus with me also.

claim.text: Paul took him to Jerusalem, and “neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised”.

quote.text: Whether any do enquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellowhelper concerning you:

claim.text: Paul “desired Titus, that as he had begun, so he would also finish in you the same grace”, and Titus went “of his own accord”.

acts.text: He went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas. Paul writes that Titus, “being a Greek”, was not “compelled to be circumcised”, and that to the “false brethren” who came in “we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour”.
When Paul came to Troas he “had no rest in my spirit, because I found not Titus my brother”, and went on into Macedonia.
In Macedonia “God … comforted us by the coming of Titus”, who brought word of the Corinthians' “earnest desire”, “mourning” and “fervent mind”; his spirit “was refreshed by you all”.
Paul sent him to Corinth to finish the collection, with “the brother, whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches” and another brother.
“Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit?”
The letter to him says: “For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city”.
Paul asks him, when Artemas or Tychicus comes, to come to Nicopolis for the winter, and to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way.
2 Timothy says he had gone “unto Dalmatia”.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Went up with Paul and Barnabas.

places.name: Troas
places.note: Paul looked for him here and did not find him.

places.name: Macedonia
places.note: Met Paul here with news from Corinth.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Paul's envoy here.

places.name: Crete
places.note: Left here to appoint elders. Called the bishop of its churches by Eusebius, about 325 (tradition).

places.name: Nicopolis
places.note: Asked to join Paul here for the winter.

places.name: Dalmatia
places.note: The last place Scripture names for him.

places.name: Gortyna, in Crete
places.note: Called its bishop in a late fragment ascribed to Zenas (tradition).

claim.text: Took him to Jerusalem, sent him to Corinth, left him in Crete; “my partner and fellowhelper”.
Went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Titus.
Paul planned to send him or Tychicus to Titus, who was then to come to Paul at Nicopolis.
The other man Paul might send to Crete.
“Zenas the lawyer”, to be sent on his way by Titus.
To be sent on his way by Titus, “that nothing be wanting unto them”.
Named beside him in 2 Timothy: Demas gone to Thessalonica, Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.

scripture.text: The last we read of him: “Titus unto Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Scripture does not say whether he reached Paul at Nicopolis, or how he died.

tradition.text: Eusebius writes that, “so it is recorded”, Timothy was first bishop at Ephesus and “Titus of the churches in Crete”.
The Apostolic Constitutions list “Of Crete, Titus” among bishops ordained in the apostles' lifetime.
tradition.when: a compilation its ANF editor places “not later than the fourth century”

tradition.text: A fragment on the life of Titus ascribed to “the lawyer Zenas” makes him bishop of Gortyna in Crete and of a royal Cretan family; McGiffert calls the tradition “late, and, of course, of little authority”, though it “accords very well with all that we know of Titus”.
tradition.who: a fragment “de Vita et Actis Titi”, as reported by McGiffert and Smith

tradition.text: Candia in Crete claims to be his burial place (McGiffert, citing Cave, 1677); Smith adds that he is “said to have been permanent bishop in the island, and to have died there at an advanced age”.
tradition.who: local tradition, reported by Cave (1677), McGiffert and Smith

writings.title: The letter to Titus (addressed to him)

questions.question: Was Titus circumcised at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3–5)? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: No: Paul did not yield
views.holders: Lightfoot (1890), with “the vast majority of early writers”; Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Lightfoot: the incident is told to show Paul never conceded circumcision, and Paul “could scarcely say ‘we yielded no not for an hour’ in the same breath” as confessing it.

views.label: Yes: he was circumcised, but not by compulsion
views.holders: Farrar (1879); Pelagius, the one early exception Lightfoot found; “several modern critics” (Lightfoot)

argument.text: Farrar asks why Paul's sentence is “so ambiguous, so involved” if he did not yield, and reads “was compelled” to mean Titus was circumcised “but not under compulsion”.

questions.question: A reading behind the question: did Paul write “no, not for an hour” (Galatians 2:5)? (Greek texts first.)

views.label: Yes, with the negative
views.holders: the Greek texts (the site's Textus Receptus and Tischendorf); the KJV and Revised Version; Jerome; Lightfoot (1890)

argument.text: Lightfoot finds the Greek texts all but unanimous (the Greek of codex D is the exception) and traces the omission to Western copies and the Old Latin version.

views.label: Without it: “For an hour we did give place”
views.holders: Irenaeus (about 180), in the Latin translation; Tertullian, Against Marcion 5.3, who accused Marcion of inserting the negative

argument.text: Irenaeus quotes “For an hour we did give place to subjection”; Tertullian argued that Paul made “some concession, as was necessary, for a time”.

questions.question: Which visit to Jerusalem took Titus with Paul (Galatians 2:1)? (Older view first.)

views.label: The council of Acts 15
views.holders: Irenaeus (about 180); Lightfoot (1890); Smith (1884); Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Lightfoot: the visit “has from the earliest times been identified with the visit recorded in Acts xv”: the same places, people and question. Rutherfurd counts Titus among “certain other of them” in Acts 15:2.

views.label: The famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay takes Titus to have been an assistant on the relief journey, and argues Paul would not have brought “an uncircumcised Greek” to the council itself.

questions.question: Why is Titus never named in Acts? (Order: the views as they appear in these sources.)

views.label: No reason can be given
views.holders: Rutherfurd, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: “It is difficult and perhaps impossible to give the true reason”.

views.label: He was Luke's relative, and Luke left him out as he left himself out
views.holders: Ramsay (1895), as a conjecture; A. Souter, as reported in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Ramsay suggests “Perhaps Titus was the relative of Luke”, while granting “There is not sufficient evidence to justify an opinion”; Souter (as reported by Robertson, ISBE 1915) reads “the brother” of 2 Corinthians 8:18 as Titus's own brother, Luke.

notSaid: Scripture does not name Titus's family or home town.
Scripture does not say when Paul and Titus were in Crete together, or whether Titus came to Nicopolis.
Scripture does not say why Titus went to Dalmatia, or what became of him.
Scripture does not call Titus a bishop.

apostles.name: Luke
apostles.title: “The beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14)
apostles.tagline: Named three times, by Paul; by early tradition the writer of the Gospel and Acts.

family.text: Paul lists Aristarchus, Marcus and Jesus called Justus as those “of the circumcision”, then names Epaphras, Luke and Demas separately.
From that list Smith (1884), Schaff (1890) and Robertson (ISBE, 1915) conclude that Luke was a Gentile.

identifications.text: Scripture names Luke three times, all in Paul's letters: Colossians 4:14, Philemon 24 (“Lucas”) and 2 Timothy 4:11. The Gospel and Acts never name their writer; both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by recalling “the former treatise”.

Irenaeus is one of the first two witnesses, with the Muratorian fragment, to name this Luke as the writer (McGiffert, 1890): “Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him”, and he argues from the “we” passages that Luke “was inseparable from Paul”.

The Muratorian fragment says “the well-known physician Luke” wrote the third Gospel “when Paul had associated him with himself”, and that “the Acts of all the Apostles are comprised by Luke in one book”.
Tertullian calls Luke “not an apostle, but only an apostolic man”, a disciple of Paul.
Smith (1884) and Robertson (ISBE, 1915) hold that Luke is not the Lucius of Acts 13:1 or Romans 16:21.

Schaff (1890) rejects the later stories that Luke was one of the Seventy or the companion of Cleopas on the road to Emmaus, because the Gospel's opening shows he was not an eyewitness; McGiffert (1890) rejects the Seventy on the same ground and calls the Emmaus idea an “ingenious but unfounded guess”.

acts.text: Paul sends greetings from “Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas”.
To Philemon Paul names “Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers”.
In 2 Timothy, a prisoner in Rome, Paul writes that Demas has forsaken him, Crescens and Titus have gone, and “Only Luke is with me”.

The narrative of Acts turns to “we” at Troas (Acts 16:10) and leaves it after Philippi (16:17); “we” returns at 20:5 and runs to Jerusalem (21:18), and again from 27:1 to Rome (28:16). The narrator is not named.

In those passages the narrator sails from Troas to Philippi and speaks to the women by the river there; sails from Philippi to Troas, Miletus, Tyre and Caesarea; goes up to Jerusalem and in “unto James”; and takes the voyage with Paul, the shipwreck at Melita and the road to Rome.

places.name: Rome
places.note: With Paul in his last imprisonment (2 Timothy).

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.note: His family's city or birthplace in Eusebius (about 325) and Jerome (about 392) (tradition).

places.name: Troas
places.note: Where “we” begins. Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.name: Philippi
places.note: Where “we” stops and starts again; Robertson (ISBE) takes it as his home. Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.name: Miletus
places.note: Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.name: Tyre

places.note: Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.note: Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.note: Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.note: Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was).

places.name: Constantinople
places.note: Where his bones were laid, says Jerome, about 392 (tradition).

claim.text: Calls him “the beloved physician” and a fellowlabourer; “Only Luke is with me”.
Named beside him twice; later “hath forsaken me”.
Sends greetings with him; Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark when “Only Luke is with me”.
A fellowlabourer named with him.
Named beside him among Paul's greeters.
The Gospel and Acts are addressed to him; he is Luke's companion only if Luke wrote them.

scripture.text: The last we read of him: “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). Scripture does not record his later life or his death.

tradition.text: Eusebius writes that Luke was “of Antiochian parentage and a physician by profession”, “especially intimate with Paul”, and that he wrote the Gospel and Acts.

Jerome calls him “a physician of Antioch” and “companion of all his journeying”, and says he “was buried at Constantinople to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantius, his bones together with the remains of Andrew the apostle were transferred”.
A list of “the Seventy” ascribed to Hippolytus makes Luke one of the Seventy, won back by Paul, and says he was “crucified on an olive tree”.
tradition.who: On the Seventy Apostles, ascribed to Hippolytus
tradition.when: date unknown; its editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”

tradition.text: Gregory of Nazianzus calls him a martyr and has him work in Achaia; Epiphanius makes him one of the Seventy and has him work in Dalmatia, Gaul, Italy and Macedonia (both as reported by McGiffert, who gives the second “about as much worth as most such traditions”).
tradition.who: Gregory of Nazianzus and Epiphanius, as reported by McGiffert
tradition.when: 4th century (their dates not checked in a source here)

tradition.text: That Luke was a painter rests, McGiffert writes, on “late tradition, of which the earlier Fathers know nothing”, found in Nicephorus and later writers.
tradition.who: Nicephorus Callistus, Church History 2.43 (as reported by McGiffert)

writings.title: The Gospel according to Luke (its traditional title)
The Acts of the Apostles (by the same tradition)

questions.question: Who is the “we” of Acts, and did Luke write the book? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Luke, Paul's companion, wrote the “we” passages and the whole of Acts
views.holders: Irenaeus (about 180); the Muratorian fragment; Ramsay (1895); Schaff (1890); Harnack (1907), as reported in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Ramsay: “It is almost universally recognised that the use of the first person … is intentional”. Harnack (Luke the Physician, 1907, as reported in the ISBE) set out the case that the “we” passages share the vocabulary and style of the rest of Luke and Acts.

views.label: The “we” passages are the work of Timothy
views.holders: Schleiermacher (1845); Sorof (1890), who gives one source to Luke and one to Timothy; both as reported in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: On this view the first-person travel account came from Timothy, who was with Paul on those journeys.

views.label: A companion's travel account, taken over by a later compiler who was not Paul's companion
views.holders: “the opposite school” described by McGiffert (1890), who points to Weizsäcker; Holtzmann, who gives Luke the “we” sections only; Schmiedel; both as reported in the ISBE (1915)

argument.text: McGiffert describes this school as “considering the ‘we’ sections authentic historical accounts from the pen of a companion of Paul, which were afterward incorporated into a larger work by one who was not a pupil of Paul”.

questions.question: Where was Luke from? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Antioch
views.holders: Eusebius (about 325); Jerome (about 392); Schaff (1890), “probably a Syrian of Antioch”

argument.text: Eusebius gives him “Antiochian parentage”; Jerome calls him “a physician of Antioch”. Schaff points to Acts' close knowledge of the church at Antioch.

views.label: Only a family link with Antioch; himself a Macedonian
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay reads Eusebius as stating only a family connection with Antioch, and suggests Luke was the “man of Macedonia” of Paul's vision.

views.label: Philippi, at least for some years
views.holders: Robertson, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: The “we” stops at Philippi and starts again there years later; Robertson concludes “we may consider Philippi as the home of Luke”.

questions.question: Is Luke “the brother, whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches” (2 Corinthians 8:18)? (Order the views arose.)

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Origen (3rd century), as quoted by Eusebius 6.25; Jerome (about 392); Ramsay (1895) (“according to an early tradition”)

argument.text: Origen speaks of “the third by Luke, the Gospel commended by Paul”; Jerome quotes 2 Corinthians 8:18 of Luke's Gospel. McGiffert (1890) answers that the verse does not refer to any written Gospel.

views.label: Yes, and Titus's own brother
views.holders: A. Souter, as reported by Robertson, ISBE (1915), who calls it “possible, even probable”

argument.text: Reading “the brother” as “his brother”, the brother of Titus named just before; that would also explain why Acts never names Titus.

notSaid: Scripture never names the writer of the Gospel of Luke or of Acts.
Scripture does not say where Luke was born or how he came to believe.
Scripture does not say that Luke met Jesus; the Gospel's opening says its writer relied on eyewitnesses (Luke 1:2).
Scripture does not record Luke's death.

apostles.name: Apollos
apostles.title: “An eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures” (Acts 18:24)
apostles.tagline: A Jew of Alexandria who watered what Paul had planted at Corinth.

home.text: “A certain Jew named Apollos, born at Alexandria”.

identifications.text: The KJV's “eloquent” renders a Greek word the Revised Version (1881) translates “learned”.
Before he met Aquila and Priscilla he “was instructed in the way of the Lord” and taught “diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John”.

How he had learned so much yet knew “only the baptism of John” is explained in different ways: Blass (as reported by Kerr) thought he had a written gospel that reached Alexandria; Kerr (ISBE, 1915) thinks it “more probably” came from what he had heard of John the Baptist's preaching.

Lightfoot (1890) holds that Apollos was not counted an apostle: Clement of Rome sets the Corinthians' partisanship for “Apostles that were highly reputed” beside partisanship for “a man approved in their sight”, meaning Apollos.

calling.label: Acts 18: taught, then sent to Achaia

quote.text: And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace:

claim.text: At Ephesus he spoke boldly in the synagogue; Aquila and Priscilla “took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly”, and the brethren commended him to Achaia.

acts.text: He came to Ephesus “fervent in the spirit” and spoke boldly in the synagogue, “knowing only the baptism of John”, until Aquila and Priscilla taught him more.
In Achaia he “helped them much which had believed through grace: For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ”.
Paul came to Ephesus “while Apollos was at Corinth”.

At Corinth some said “I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ”. Paul answers: “Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed”; “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase”.
Paul writes that he has applied these things “in a figure” to himself and Apollos, “that no one of you be puffed up for one against another”.
“As touching our brother Apollos, I greatly desired him to come unto you with the brethren: but his will was not at all to come at this time; but he will come when he shall have convenient time.”
Later Paul asks Titus to “Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them”.

places.name: Alexandria
places.note: His birthplace.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Taught by Aquila and Priscilla. Paul, writing 1 Corinthians from here, had urged him to go to Corinth.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Watered what Paul had planted.

places.name: Crete
places.note: Titus, in Crete, is to send him on his way (where Apollos was going is not said).

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: Called its bishop in a list ascribed to Hippolytus (tradition); which Caesarea is not said.

claim.text: Heard him at Ephesus and taught him “the way of God more perfectly”.
“I have planted, Apollos watered”; Paul urged him to go to Corinth and calls him “our brother”.
Named with him and Paul among the Corinthians' factions.
Travelling with him when Paul wrote to Titus.
Asked to send him on his way.

scripture.text: The last we read of him: on a journey, to be helped on his way by Titus (Titus 3:13). Scripture does not record his later life or death.

tradition.text: A list of “the Seventy” ascribed to Hippolytus names “Apollo, bishop of Cæsarea”. Its ANF editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”.
tradition.who: On the Seventy Apostles, ascribed to Hippolytus

tradition.text: Smith (1884) repeats it: “Tradition makes him bishop of Caesarea”.

questions.question: Did Apollos write the Letter to the Hebrews? (In the order the views arose.)

views.label: Possibly: he fits the description of the writer
views.holders: first proposed by Luther; Alford, Kurtz and Farrar, as listed by Westcott (1892)

argument.text: Westcott: Luther “conjectured that it was more likely to have been written by Apollos”; the sole ground is the description of Apollos in Acts 18:24–28 and 1 Corinthians.

views.label: There is no evidence for it
views.holders: Westcott (1892); Easton (1897), “without sufficient ground”

argument.text: Westcott: “there is not the least evidence that Apollos wrote anything”, and the wide acceptance of the guess shows “our natural unwillingness to frankly confess our ignorance”.

notSaid: Scripture does not say how Apollos first learned “the way of the Lord”, or whether he was baptized again.
Scripture does not say that Apollos encouraged the party that used his name at Corinth.
Scripture does not say why he would not go to Corinth when Paul asked him (1 Corinthians 16:12).
Scripture does not record his later life or death; it does not say he wrote anything.

apostles.name: Priscilla and Aquila
apostles.title: Paul's “helpers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3)
apostles.tagline: A tentmaking couple who sheltered Paul, taught Apollos and kept a church in their house.

home.text: Aquila was “a certain Jew … born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:)”.

trade.text: Tentmakers: Paul “was of the same craft”, so “he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers”.

family.text: Husband and wife: “Aquila … with his wife Priscilla”.

Scripture never names one without the other. In the KJV Priscilla is named first three times out of six (Acts 18:18; Romans 16:3; 2 Timothy 4:19); in the site's Tischendorf Greek text and the Revised Version, four times, because they also put her first at Acts 18:26.

identifications.text: Acts always says Priscilla; 2 Timothy 4:19 says Prisca. In Romans 16:3 and 1 Corinthians 16:19 the KJV and the Textus Receptus read Priscilla, where Tischendorf's text and the Revised Version read Prisca.
The Roman biographer Suetonius records of Claudius: “Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome.”

Ramsay (1895) and Kapp (ISBE, 1915) take this to be the order of Acts 18:2, and “Chrestus” as a garbled reference to Christ or his followers. Ramsay adds, from Dio Cassius, that the order was hard to enforce.
Harnack proposed Priscilla, with Aquila, as the writer of Hebrews; Dods (1897, 1910 printing) reports the case and answers that the writer speaks as one man.

calling.label: Acts 18: Paul finds them at Corinth

quote.text: And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.

claim.text: Paul came to Corinth from Athens and “found a certain Jew named Aquila”; he lodged and worked with the couple. Acts does not say when they became believers.

acts.text: At Corinth Paul lived and worked with them.
When Paul left Corinth they sailed with him; he “left them” at Ephesus.
At Ephesus they heard Apollos in the synagogue, “took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly”.
From Ephesus they sent greetings to Corinth “with the church that is in their house”.

In Romans Paul greets them: “my helpers in Christ Jesus: Who have for my life laid down their own necks: unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles”, and the church in their house.
In 2 Timothy Paul asks Timothy to “Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus”.
Acts 18:18 says “having shorn his head in Cenchrea: for he had a vow”; the KJV's “his” is a supplied word, and the verse does not say plainly whether Paul or Aquila made the vow.

places.name: Pontus
places.note: Aquila's birthplace.

places.name: Rome
places.note: Left under Claudius's order; greeted here later.

places.name: Italy
places.note: “lately come from Italy”.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: Worked with Paul as tentmakers.

places.name: Cenchreae
places.note: Port of Corinth; the vow.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Taught Apollos; a church in their house.

places.name: Asia
places.note: The Apostolic Constitutions (4th century or earlier) name Aquila a bishop of “the parishes of Asia” (tradition).

claim.text: Lodged and worked with them; they risked their necks for his life.
They took him aside and taught him “the way of God more perfectly”.
Paul asks him to greet them.
His household is greeted beside them.

scripture.text: The last we read of them: Paul asks Timothy to greet them (2 Timothy 4:19). Scripture does not record their deaths.

tradition.text: The Apostolic Constitutions list “Of the parishes of Asia, Aquila and Nicetas” among bishops ordained in the apostles' lifetime.
tradition.when: a compilation its ANF editor places “not later than the fourth century”

questions.question: Why is Priscilla so often named before her husband? (Older view first.)

views.label: She was the more energetic, or stronger, of the two
views.holders: Conybeare and Howson (1891); Kapp, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Conybeare and Howson: the order “conveys the impression that she was the more energetic character of the two”; Kapp: “The best explanation seems to be that she was the stronger character.”

views.label: She was of higher rank, and it was the custom among their friends
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay: “Probably Prisca was of higher rank than her husband, for her name is that of a good old Roman family”; the order was “a conversational custom”.

questions.question: Were they already believers when Paul met them? (Order: as in these sources.)

views.label: No: they came to faith through Paul at Corinth
views.holders: Conybeare and Howson (1891); Kapp, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Acts gives the reason Paul joined them as their common trade, not a common faith; Conybeare and Howson think conversion at Rome “probably not the case”.

views.label: Acts does not say; it may have been at Rome
views.holders: Easton (1897); Smith (1884); Conybeare and Howson allow that it is possible

argument.text: Easton: “When they became Christians we are not informed”; Smith: “At what time they became Christians is uncertain.”

questions.question: Who made the vow at Cenchrea (Acts 18:18)? (Order: as in these sources.)

views.label: Aquila
views.holders: Conybeare and Howson (1891), in their text, “left as it stood in the earlier editions”

argument.text: They describe Aquila ending a Jewish vow before sailing; their own note admits that “the arguments from the structure of the original are rather in favour of referring the vow, not to Aquila, but to St. Paul”.

views.label: Paul
views.holders: Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay: “Though the grammatical construction of v. 18 would suggest that Aquila made the vow … the natural emphasis marks Paul as the subject here.”

questions.question: When did Claudius order the Jews out of Rome (Acts 18:2)? Suetonius gives no year. (Earliest date first.)

views.label: AD 49, Claudius's ninth year
views.holders: Orosius, as reported by Ramsay (1895)

argument.text: Ramsay reports that “Orosius says that it occurred in Claudius's ninth year, 49”.

views.label: AD 50
views.holders: Easton (1897); Ramsay (1895), who puts it at “the end of 50”

argument.text: Ramsay judges Orosius's date “a year wrong” and puts Aquila in Corinth some months before Paul.

views.label: AD 52
views.holders: Kapp, ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Kapp dates the edict that expelled the Jews to 52.

notSaid: Scripture does not say when or where Priscilla and Aquila came to believe.
Scripture does not say how they risked their necks for Paul (Romans 16:4).
Scripture does not say which of them made the vow at Cenchrea, or that either of them wrote anything.
Scripture does not record their later life or deaths.
